{{ill|Hinokuma no Hamanari|WD=Q123219585}}; {{ill|Hinokuma no Takenari|WD=Q123219599}}|deity={{ill|Avalokiteśvara|WD=Q193849}}|part_of={{ill|Bandō Sanjūsankasho|WD=Q806417}}; {{ill|Edo Sanjūsankasho|WD=Q11550981}}; {{ill|Q11557223|WD=Q11557223}}; {{ill|Three Major Kannon Temples in Japan|WD=Q11507116}}}}{{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q615183]] Wikidata name: Sensō-ji [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:12, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Short description|Buddhist temple in Tokyo, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Sensō-ji | native_name = | image = Sensoji 2023.jpg | alt = | caption = Sensō-ji Main Hall in 2023 | map_type = Japan | map_size = | map_alt = | map_caption = | location = 2-3-1 Asakusa, [[:en:Taitō, Tokyo|Taitō-ku, Tokyo]] | coordinates = {{coord|35.714722|139.79675|type:landmark|display=title,inline}} | religious_affiliation = {{ill|Buddhism|en|Buddhism|WD=Q748|lt=Buddhism}} | sect = Shō-Kannon (independent school) | deity = {{ill|Avalokiteśvara|en|Avalokiteśvara|WD=Q193849|lt=Shō Kannon Bosatsu}}
(Āryāvalokiteśvara) | country = Japan | functional_status = | website = {{URL|www.senso-ji.jp}} | founded_by = Kaishō | year_completed = 645 }} {{nihongo|'''Sensō-ji'''|浅草寺 {{IPA|ja|sẽ̞ꜜɰ̃so̞ːʑi||TomJ-SensoJi.ogg}}|Sensō-ji|4=officially {{Nihongo|'''Kinryū-zan Sensō-ji'''|金龍山浅草寺}}, also known as {{Nihongo|'''Asakusa Kannon'''|浅草観音}}}}, is an ancient {{ill|Buddhist temples in Japan|en|Buddhist temples in Japan|WD=Q3141900|lt=Buddhist temple}} in [[Asakusa]], Tokyo, Japan. It is Tokyo's oldest-established temple, and one of its most significant. It is dedicated to [[Kannon|Kannon]], the {{ill|Bodhisattva|en|Bodhisattva|WD=Q178149|lt=Bodhisattva}} of compassion. Structures in the temple complex include the main hall, a five-story {{ill|Pagoda|en|Pagoda|WD=Q199451|lt=Pagoda}} and large gates. It is the most widely visited religious site in the world with over 30 million visitors annually.{{Cite web |url= http://www.travelandleisure.com/slideshows/worlds-most-visited-sacred-sites |title=World's Most-Visited Sacred Sites}}{{Cite web |url= http://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2014/07/07/national/asakusa-paints-traditional-tokyo-popular-light/#.WNrv7nTyut8 |title = Asakusa paints traditional Tokyo in a popular light|date = 7 July 2014}} The temple was destroyed during a {{ill|Bombing of Tokyo (10 March 1945)|en|Bombing of Tokyo (10 March 1945)|WD=Q51881408|lt=10 March 1945 firebombing air raid on Tokyo}} during {{ill|Pacific War|en|Pacific War|WD=Q184425|lt=Pacific War}}. The main hall was rebuilt in the 1950s. Formerly associated with the {{ill|Tendai|en|Tendai|WD=Q855964|lt=Tendai}} {{ill|Sect|en|Sect|WD=Q19097|lt=Sect}} of {{ill|Buddhism|en|Buddhism|WD=Q748|lt=Buddhism}}, the temple became independent after the war. Leading to it is Nakamise-dōri street, containing many shops with traditional goods.{{Cite web |url= https://planetyze.com/en/japan/tokyo/sensoji-temple |title=Sensoji Temple - Tokyo Travel Guide {{!}} Planetyze|website=Planetyze|language=en|access-date=2017-06-27}} Adjacent to the east of Sensō-ji is the [[Asakusa Shrine]] of the [[Shinto]] religion.{{cite web |url= https://www.gojapango.com/places/tokyo/tokyo/temple/sensoji-temple/ |title=Sensō-ji |publisher=GoJapanGo |access-date=2008-10-23|archive-date=2017-03-28 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20170328043928/https://www.gojapango.com/places/tokyo/tokyo/temple/sensoji-temple/|url-status=dead}} == History == [[File:Dai Nippon Kinryū-zan no Zu, Aōdō Denzen, 1809.jpg|thumb|left|300px|Colored print of Sensō-ji temple, by Aōdō Denzen (亜欧堂田善), circa 1809]] The temple is dedicated to the {{ill|Bodhisattva|en|Bodhisattva|WD=Q178149|lt=Bodhisattva}} [[Kannon|Kannon]] ({{ill|Avalokiteśvara|en|Avalokiteśvara|WD=Q193849|lt=Avalokiteśvara}}). According to legend, a statue of the Kannon was found in the {{ill|Sumida River|en|Sumida River|WD=Q222149|lt=Sumida River}} in 628 AD by two fishermen, brothers Hinokuma Hamanari and Hinokuma Takenari. The chief of their village, Hajino Nakamoto, recognized the sanctity of the statue and enshrined it by remodeling his own house into a small temple in Asakusa so that the villagers could worship Kannon.{{cite web|url=http://www.cse.sc.edu/~jimdavis/Personal/Photographs/Japan2001-SensojiTemple/Sensoji_temple-Sept01.htm|title=Senso-ji (Pure Land) Buddhist Temple, Asakusa, Tokyo, Japan|last=Davis|first=James P.|date=September 2001|publisher=University of South Carolina|access-date=2008-10-23|archive-date=2012-07-29|archive-url=https://archive.today/20120729094515/http://www.cse.sc.edu/~jimdavis/Personal/Photographs/Japan2001-SensojiTemple/Sensoji_temple-Sept01.htm|url-status=dead}} The first temple was founded in 645 AD, which makes it the oldest-established temple in Tokyo.[http://www.worldgreatestsites.com/sensoji.htm World's greatest sites] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080318103100/http://www.worldgreatestsites.com/sensoji.htm |date=2008-03-18 }} accessed May 2, 2008 In the early years of the [[Tokugawa shogunate]], {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|WD=Q171977|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu}} designated Sensō-ji as {{ill|Tutelary deity|en|Tutelary deity|WD=Q3032312|lt=tutelary temple}} of the [[Tokugawa clan]].McClain, James ''et al.'' (1997). [https://books.google.com/books?id=3N5d4xKg7yQC&dq=Sensoji&pg=PA86 ''Edo and Paris,'' p. 86.] During World War II, the temple was destroyed during the {{ill|Bombing of Tokyo (10 March 1945)|en|Bombing of Tokyo (10 March 1945)|WD=Q51881408|lt=10 March 1945 firebombing air raid on Tokyo}}. The main hall was rebuilt in 1951–58 and has been perceived as a symbol of rebirth and peace by Japanese people. In the courtyard there is a tree that was hit by a bomb in the air raids, and it had regrown in the husk of the old tree and is a similar symbol as the temple itself.{{Citation needed|date=December 2023}} The temple now has a titanium tiled roof that maintains a historic image but is stronger and lighter.{{Cite news |url= https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2009/05/25/national/nippon-steel-pitches-roof-tiles-made-of-titanium/ |title=Nippon Steel pitches roof tiles made of titanium |date=2009-05-25|work=The Japan Times Online|access-date=2019-02-18|language=en-US|issn=0447-5763}} The {{ill|Kaminarimon|en|Kaminarimon|WD=Q2378708|lt=Kaminarimon}} gate was rebuilt in 1960, the {{ill|Hōzōmon|en|Hōzōmon|WD=Q2378896|lt=Hōzōmon}} gate in 1964, and the pagoda in 1973.{{cite web |title=Sensoji Temple – The Heart of Asakusa |url= https://www.asakusastation.com/sensoji-temple-the-heart-of-asakusa/ |website=Asakusa Station |access-date=6 March 2024}} The [[Nishinomiya Inari shrine]] was located within the precincts of Sensō-ji and a [[torii]] identified the entry into the hallowed ground of the shrine. A bronze plaque on the gateway structure listed those who contributed to the construction of the torii, which was erected in 1727 (''{{ill|Kyōhō|en|Kyōhō|WD=Q1145048|lt=Kyōhō}} 12, 11th month'').McClain, [https://books.google.com/books?id=-qOuykzxhKUC&dq=Sensoji&pg=PA403 p. 403.] After the {{ill|Government of Meiji Japan|en|Government of Meiji Japan|WD=Q1322181|lt=Meiji government}} ordered the [[shinbutsu bunri|separation of Shinto and Buddhism]] in 1868, the Inari shrine was moved to the grounds of the [[Asakusa Shrine]], where it was destroyed in the 10 March 1945 firebombing.{{cite web |title=Event: Praying for Success in Business at Asakusa Hatsuka-Ebisu 2023 |first= |last= |date=23 January 2023 |url= https://everywhere.tokyo/en/event-asakusa-hatsuka-ebisu-2023/ |work=Tokyo Shitamachi Guide |publisher= |access-date=13 April 2024}} ==Temple grounds== [[File:Sensoji 2012.JPG|thumb|left|The green-roofed shops of Nakamise-dōri leading to the temple]] Sensō-ji is the focus of Tokyo's largest and most popular [[Japanese festivals|festival]], {{ill|Sanja Matsuri|en|Sanja Matsuri|WD=Q219122|lt=Sanja Matsuri}}. This takes place over 3 to 4 days in late spring, and sees the surrounding streets closed to traffic from dawn until late evening.{{Citation needed|date=December 2023}} Dominating the entrance to the temple is the {{ill|Kaminarimon|en|Kaminarimon|WD=Q2378708|lt=Kaminarimon}} or "Thunder Gate". This imposing Buddhist structure features a massive paper lantern dramatically painted in vivid red-and-black tones to suggest thunderclouds and lightning. Beyond the Kaminarimon is Nakamise-dori with its shops, followed by the {{ill|Hōzōmon|en|Hōzōmon|WD=Q2378896|lt=Hōzōmon}} or "Treasure House Gate", which provides the entrance to the inner complex. Within the precincts stand a stately five-story {{ill|Pagoda|en|Pagoda|WD=Q199451|lt=Pagoda}} and the main hall, devoted to Kannon.{{cite web|url=http://www.worldtravelguide.net/attraction/409/attraction_guide/Far-East-Asia/Senso-ji-Temple-Kinryuzan-Senso-ji.html|title=Senso-ji Temple (Kinryuzan Senso-ji) Guide |publisher=World Travel Guide|access-date=2009-02-07}} Many tourists, both Japanese and from abroad, visit Sensō-ji every year. Catering to the visiting crowds, the surrounding area has many traditional shops and eating places that feature traditional dishes (hand-made noodles, sushi, tempura, etc.). Nakamise-Dori, the street leading from the Thunder Gate to the temple itself, is lined with small shops selling souvenirs ranging from fans, ''[[ukiyo-e]]'' ({{ill|Woodblock printing|en|Woodblock printing|WD=Q1261053|lt=woodblock prints}}), {{ill|Kimono|en|Kimono|WD=Q483444|lt=Kimono}} and other robes, Buddhist scrolls, traditional sweets, to {{ill|Godzilla|en|Godzilla|WD=Q6567|lt=Godzilla}} toys, t-shirts and mobile phone straps. These shops themselves are part of a living tradition of selling to pilgrims who walked to Sensō-ji.{{Citation needed|date=December 2023}} Within the temple itself, and also at many places on its approach, there are ''{{ill|O-mikuji|en|O-mikuji|WD=Q1069592|lt=O-mikuji}}'' stalls. For a suggested donation of 100 yen, visitors may consult the oracle and divine answers to their questions. Querents shake labelled sticks from enclosed metal containers and read the corresponding answers they retrieve from one of 100 possible drawers.{{Citation needed|date=December 2023}} Within the temple is a quiet contemplative garden kept in the distinctive {{ill|Japanese garden|en|Japanese garden|WD=Q15835|lt=Japanese style}}.{{Citation needed|date=December 2023}} === Kaminarimon === [[File:Sensoji at night 8.jpg|thumb|right|Kaminarimon. A statue of [[Fūjin]] stands on the right and that of [[Raijin]] on the left.]] The {{nihongo|{{ill|Kaminarimon|en|Kaminarimon|WD=Q2378708|lt=Kaminarimon}}|雷門|"Thunder Gate"}} is the outer of two large entrance gates that ultimately lead to the Sensō-ji (the inner being the Hōzōmon) in [[Asakusa]]. The gate, with its lantern and statues, is popular with tourists. It stands {{convert|11.7|m|ft}} tall, {{convert|11.4|m|ft}} wide and covers an area of {{convert|69.3|m2|sqft}}.{{cite web|url=http://www7.ocn.ne.jp/~sehayama/topics4kaminarimon.htm|language=ja|script-title=ja:雷門|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080224224816/http://www7.ocn.ne.jp/~sehayama/topics4kaminarimon.htm|archive-date=February 24, 2008|url-status=dead|access-date=2008-03-07|df=mdy-all}} The first gate was built in 941, but the current gate dates back to 1960, after the previous gate was destroyed in a fire in 1865.{{Citation needed|date=December 2023}} ==== History ==== The Kaminarimon was first built in 941 AD by [[Taira clan|Taira]] no Kinmasa, a military commander.{{cite web|url=http://www.taitocity.com/kanko/asakusa_ueno/e_guide/tour/spots/kaminarimon.html|title=Kaminarimon Gate|access-date=2008-03-07|archive-date=2008-03-18|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080318103831/http://www.taitocity.com/kanko/asakusa_ueno/e_guide/tour/spots/kaminarimon.html|url-status=dead}} It was originally located near Komagata, but it was reconstructed in its current location in 1635. This is believed to be when the gods of wind and thunder were first placed on the gate. The gate has been destroyed many times throughout the ages. Four years after its relocation, the Kaminarimon burned down, and in 1649 AD {{ill|Tokugawa Iemitsu|en|Tokugawa Iemitsu|WD=Q314481|lt=Tokugawa Iemitsu}} rebuilt the gate along with several other of the major structures in the temple complex.{{cite web|url=http://www.asakusa-umai.ne.jp/e_asakusa/matsuri/matsuri-02_e.html|title=Glossary of Terms|access-date=2008-03-07}} The gate burnt to the ground in 1757 AD and again in 1865 AD. The Kaminarimon's current structure was dedicated in December 1960 AD . Ninety-five years after the last fire, [[:en:Konosuke Matsushita|Konosuke Matsushita]], the founder of Matsushita Electric Industrial Company (now {{ill|Panasonic|en|Panasonic|WD=Q53247|lt=Panasonic}}), was asked to rebuild the gate. With monetary donations from Matsushita, it was rebuilt in 1960.{{cite web|url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2013/11/18/national/famed-kaminarimon-lantern-gets-rare-makeover/|title=Famed Kaminarimon lantern gets rare makeover|date=November 18, 2013|work=[[The Japan Times]]|access-date=March 22, 2019|agency=[[Kyodo News]]}} ==== Features ==== [[File:Kaminarimon_lantern_bottom_2006.JPG|right|thumb|The wooden carving of a {{ill|Japanese dragon|en|Japanese dragon|WD=Q2366503|lt=dragon}} on the bottom of the great red {{ill|paper lantern|en|paper lantern|WD=Q9545439|lt=lantern}} on the Kaminarimon]] Four statues are housed in the Kaminarimon, two in the front alcoves and two on the other side. On the front of the gate, the statues of the [[Shinto]] gods [[Fūjin]] and [[Raijin]] are displayed. Fūjin, the god of wind, is located on the east side of the gate, while Raijin, the god of thunder, is located on the west side. The original sculptures were severely damaged in the fire of 1865, with only the heads being saved, and the statues restored for the gate's 1960 reconstruction.Enbutsu, Sumiko. ''Old Tokyo: Walks in the City of the Shogun''. Tokyo: Tuttle, 2012 Two additional statues stand on the reverse of the gate: the {{ill|Buddhism|en|Buddhism|WD=Q748|lt=Buddhist}} god Tenryū on the east, and the goddess Kinryū on the west side. These were donated in 1978 to commemorate the 1350th anniversary of the first appearance of the {{ill|Bodhisattva|en|Bodhisattva|WD=Q178149|lt=Bodhisattva}} [[Kannon|Kannon]] ({{ill|Avalokiteśvara|en|Avalokiteśvara|WD=Q193849|lt=Avalokiteśvara}}) at Asakusa, which led to the founding of Sensō-ji. The statues were carved by then-106-year-old master sculptor {{ill|Hirakushi Denchū|en|Hirakushi Denchū|WD=Q11483145|lt=Hirakushi Denchū}}. A giant red lantern (''[[Traditional lighting equipment of Japan#Chōchin|chōchin]]'') hangs under the center of the gate. It is {{convert|3.9|m|ft}} tall, {{convert|3.3|m|ft}} wide and weighs approximately {{convert|700|kg|lb}}. The current lantern, the fifth iteration, was built by Takahashi Chōchin K.K in 2013 and has the same metallic base on the bottom as the previous lantern. The base has a name plate that says "Matsushita Denki", an abbreviated form of Panasonic's old Japanese name, Matsushita Denki Sangyo Kabushiki Gaisha. The front of the lantern displays the gate's name, {{nihongo|Kaminarimon|雷門}}. Painted on the back is the gate's official name, {{nihongo|Fūraijinmon|風雷神門}}.{{cite web|url=http://www.asakusa-e.com/rekisi/senso_e.htm|title=Sensoji Temple|access-date=2008-03-07}} During festivals such as {{ill|Sanja Matsuri|en|Sanja Matsuri|WD=Q219122|lt=Sanja Matsuri}}, the lantern is collapsed to let tall objects pass through the gate. The characters {{Nihongo|金龍山|Kinryū-zan}} on the tablet above the lantern read from right to left and reference the Sensō-ji. === Hōzōmon === [[File:Hozomon_on_an_overcast_day_dllu.jpg|right|thumb|The south face of the Hōzōmon]] The {{nihongo|{{ill|Hōzōmon|en|Hōzōmon|WD=Q2378896|lt=Hōzōmon}}|宝蔵門|"Treasure-House Gate"}} is the inner of two large entrance gates that lead to the Sensō-ji. It is a two-story gate (''{{ill|Nijūmon|en|Nijūmon|WD=Q3341490|lt=Nijūmon}}''), and its second story houses many of the Sensō-ji's treasures. The first story houses two statues, three lanterns and two large sandals. It stands {{convert|22.7|m|ft}} tall, {{convert|21|m|ft}} wide, and {{convert|8|m|ft}} deep.{{cite web|url=http://www7.ocn.ne.jp/~sehayama/topics6houzou5juu.htm|language=ja|script-title=ja:宝蔵門・五重搭・不動尊|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080229002310/http://www7.ocn.ne.jp/~sehayama/topics6houzou5juu.htm|archive-date=2008-02-29|url-status=dead|access-date=2008-03-30}} ==== History ==== [[File:Hozomon_sensoji_back.jpg|thumb|The gate's north face]] The Hōzōmon was first built in 942 AD by [[Taira clan|Taira]] no Kinmasa.{{cite web|url=http://www.asakusa-e.com/rekisi/senso_e.htm|title=Sensoji Temple|work=asakusa-e.com|access-date=2008-03-30}} Destroyed by fire in 1631, it was rebuilt by {{ill|Tokugawa Iemitsu|en|Tokugawa Iemitsu|WD=Q314481|lt=Tokugawa Iemitsu}} in 1636. It stood for 300 more years until it was once again burned down during the [[:en:Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of 1945]]. In 1964, the present steel-reinforced concrete structure was built with a donation of [[:en:Yen|¥]]150 million from Yonetarō Motoya. Since the gate was reconstructed using flame-resistant materials, the upper story of the Hōzōmon stores the Sensō-ji's treasured {{ill|Sutra|en|Sutra|WD=Q209680|lt=sutras}}. These treasures include a copy of the {{ill|en:Lotus Sutra|en|en:Lotus Sutra|WD=Q861212|lt=en:Lotus Sutra}} that is designated a [[:en:National treasures of Japan|Japanese National Treasure]] and the ''Issai-kyō'', a complete collection of {{ill|Buddhism|en|Buddhism|WD=Q748|lt=Buddhist}} scriptures that has been designated an {{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|en|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|WD=Q1188622|lt=Important Cultural Property}}.{{cite web|url=http://www.asakusa-umai.ne.jp/e_asakusa/matsuri/matsuri-02_e.html|title=Glossary of Terms|access-date=2008-03-30}} ==== Features ==== [[File:Shukongoshin.JPG|thumb|One of the {{ill|Nio (Buddhism)|en|Nio (Buddhism)|WD=Q539715|lt=Nio (Buddhism)}} statues that stand on either side of the gate's south face]] Unlike the Kaminarimon, which houses four different statues, the Hōzōmon houses two guardian statues that are located on either side of the gate's south face. These {{convert|5.45|m|ft}} tall statues represent {{ill|Nio (Buddhism)|en|Nio (Buddhism)|WD=Q539715|lt=Nio (Buddhism)}}, the guardian deities of the [[:en:Gautama Buddha|Buddha]]. Because of these statues, the gate was originally called the {{nihongo|''{{ill|Niōmon|en|Niōmon|WD=Q3342330|lt=Niōmon}}''|仁王門|"Niō Gate"}} before it was renamed the Hōzōmon. The gate also features three large lanterns. The largest and most prominent lantern is a red ''[[Traditional lighting equipment of Japan#Chōchin|chōchin]]'' that hangs under the center of the gate's opening. With a height of {{convert|3.75|m|ft}}, a diameter of {{convert|2.7|m|ft}} and a weight of {{convert|400|kg|lbs}}, the lantern displays the name of the town {{nihongo|Kobunachō|小舟町}}. The current iteration of the lantern dates back to 2003 when ¥2 billion was donated by the people of Kobunachō. Its donation commemorated the 10th-year-anniversary of the start of the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}. On either side of the ''chōchin'' hangs five {{convert|2.75|m|ft}} tall copper ''[[Traditional lighting equipment of Japan#Tōrō|tōrō]]'' weighing approximately {{convert|1000|kg|lbs}} each. All three lanterns are completely removed during festivals such as {{ill|Sanja Matsuri|en|Sanja Matsuri|WD=Q219122|lt=Sanja Matsuri}}. On the Hōzōmon's east (back) face are the ''{{ill|Waraji|en|Waraji|WD=Q696696|lt=Waraji}}'', two {{convert|4.5|m|ft}} long, {{convert|1.5|m|ft}} wide straw sandals that weigh {{convert|400|kg|lbs}} each.{{cite web|url=http://www7.ocn.ne.jp/~sehayama/oteratojinnja.htm|language=ja|script-title=ja:浅草神社と浅草寺の説明|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080207085132/http://www7.ocn.ne.jp/~sehayama/oteratojinnja.htm|archive-date=2008-02-07|url-status=dead|access-date=2008-03-30}} ==Nakamise-dōri== [[File:Nakamise dori.jpg|thumb|Nakamise-dōri at night]] [[File:Nakamise street 2020-04-19.jpg|thumb|Nakamise-dōri under the state of emergency for coronavirus pandemic in 2020]] The {{nihongo|'''Nakamise-dōri'''|仲見世通り||}} is a street on the approach to the temple. It is said to have come about in the early 12th century, when neighbors of Sensō-ji were granted permission to set up shops on the approach to the temple. However, in May 1885 the government of Tokyo ordered all shop owners to leave. In December of that same year the area was reconstructed in Western-style brick. During the [[:en:1923 Great Kantō earthquake|1923 Great Kantō earthquake]] many of the shops were destroyed, then rebuilt in 1925 using concrete, only to be destroyed again during the bombings of World War II. The street is approximately {{convert|250|m|ft}} long and contains around 72 shops.[http://www.asakusa-nakamise.jp/e-index.html Asakusa-Nakamise:] [http://www.asakusa-nakamise.jp/e-history.html History of Nakamise.] ==Gallery== File:Nakamise1411.jpg|Pilgrims and tourists flocking to Sensō-ji have shopped at the small stores here for centuries. File:Sensoji at night.JPG|The temple during nighttime File:Asakusa - Senso-ji 35 (15576702197).jpg File:Sensō-ji - Ceiling - August 2013 - Sarah Stierch 02.JPG File:Sensoji Dragon Fountain.JPG File:Sensoji temple meiji era monochrome1910.jpg|1910 File:Toto_Kinryuzan_Senso-ji_zu_02.jpg|1820 File:100 views edo 039.jpg|[[Hiroshige]] File:View of mikoshi from sensoji Sanja Matsuri 2006-3.jpg|{{ill|Sanja Matsuri|en|Sanja Matsuri|WD=Q219122|lt=Sanja Matsuri}} File:Bosatsu Kannon from Simida River 02.JPG|An illustration window in Sensoji of how the two fishermen brothers find {{ill|Bosatsu|en|Bosatsu|WD=Q23925162|lt=Bosatsu}} [[Kannon]] statuette in {{ill|Sumida River|en|Sumida River|WD=Q222149|lt=Sumida River}} File:Bosatsu Kannon from Simida River 01.JPG|An illustration window in Sensoji of {{ill|Bosatsu|en|Bosatsu|WD=Q23925162|lt=Bosatsu}} [[Kannon]] consecrated and worshiped in early Senso-ji and [[Asakusa Shrine]] File:Photo-TokyoAirRaids-1945-3-10-Destroyed Nakamise-4.png|Nakamise-Dori after the American bombings of 1945 == See also == * {{ill|Buddhist temples in Japan|en|Buddhist temples in Japan|WD=Q3141900|lt=Buddhist temples in Japan}} * [[Glossary of Japanese Buddhism]] * {{ill|List of Buddhist temples|en|List of Buddhist temples|WD=Q6808012|lt=List of Buddhist temples}} * [[:en:en:List of National Treasures of Japan (writings)|en:List of National Treasures of Japan (writings)]] == Notes == {{Reflist}} ==References== * McClain, James L., John M. Merriman, Kaoru Ugawa and Ugawa Kaoru. (1997). [https://books.google.com/books?id=-qOuykzxhKUC ''Edo and Paris: Urban Life and the State in the Early Modern Era.''] Ithaca: {{ill|Cornell University Press|en|Cornell University Press|WD=Q2997531|lt=Cornell University Press}}. {{ISBN|978-0-8014-8183-3}}; [http://www.worldcat.org/wcpa/oclc/39088759 OCLC 39088759] ==External links== {{Commons Category|Sensoji|Sensō-ji}} * {{Official website|https://www.senso-ji.jp/english/}} {{Buddhist temples in Japan}} {{Taitō, Tokyo}}]]]] [[en:Sensō-ji]] [[arz:سينسو جى]] [[de:Sensō-ji]] [[el:Σένσο-τζι]] [[es:Sensō-ji]] [[eu:Sensō-ji]] [[fa:معبد سنسوجی]] [[fi:Sensō-ji]] [[fr:Sensō-ji]] [[gl:Sensō-ji]] [[hi:सेन्सो-जी]] [[hu:Szenszódzsi]] [[id:Sensō-ji]] [[it:Sensō-ji]] [[ja:浅草寺]] [[ko:센소지]] [[pl:Sensō-ji]] [[pt:Templo Sensoji]] [[ro:Sensō-ji]] [[ru:Сэнсо-дзи]] [[sh:Sensō-ji]] [[simple:Sensō-ji]] [[sl:Senso-dži]] [[sv:Sensoji]] [[th:เซ็นโซจิ]] [[tr:Sensō-ji]] [[uk:Монастир Сенсо]] [[vi:Chùa Sensō]] [[war:Sensō-ji]] [[zh:淺草寺]] [[zh-min-nan:Chhián-chháu-sī]] {{wikidata link|Q615183}} [[Category:Asakusa]] [[Category:Buddhist temples in Tokyo]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Japan destroyed during World War II]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Taitō]] [[Category:Pages with simple english wikipedia interwikis]] [[Category:Temples of Avalokiteśvara]] [[Category:Tokyo Metropolitan Designated Tangible Cultural Property]] [[Category:Wikidata has English label]] [[Category:Wikidata has short description]] [[Category:Pages with unclosed square brackets]]

{{ill|Hinokuma no Hamanari|WD=Q123219585}}; {{ill|Hinokuma no Takenari|WD=Q123219599}}|deity={{ill|Avalokiteśvara|WD=Q193849}}|part_of={{ill|Bandō Sanjūsankasho|WD=Q806417}}; {{ill|Edo Sanjūsankasho|WD=Q11550981}}; {{ill|Q11557223|WD=Q11557223}}; {{ill|Three Major Kannon Temples in Japan|WD=Q11507116}}}}{{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q615183]] Wikidata name: Sensō-ji [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:12, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Short description|Buddhist temple in Tokyo, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Sensō-ji | native_name = | image = Sensoji 2023.jpg | alt = | caption = Sensō-ji Main Hall in 2023 | map_type = Japan | map_size = | map_alt = | map_caption = | location = 2-3-1 Asakusa, [[:en:Taitō, Tokyo|Taitō-ku, Tokyo]] | coordinates = {{coord|35.714722|139.79675|type:landmark|display=title,inline}} | religious_affiliation = {{ill|Buddhism|en|Buddhism|WD=Q748|lt=Buddhism}} | sect = Shō-Kannon (independent school) | deity = {{ill|Avalokiteśvara|en|Avalokiteśvara|WD=Q193849|lt=Shō Kannon Bosatsu}}
(Āryāvalokiteśvara) | country = Japan | functional_status = | website = {{URL|www.senso-ji.jp}} | founded_by = Kaishō | year_completed = 645 }} {{nihongo|'''Sensō-ji'''|浅草寺 {{IPA|ja|sẽ̞ꜜɰ̃so̞ːʑi||TomJ-SensoJi.ogg}}|Sensō-ji|4=officially {{Nihongo|'''Kinryū-zan Sensō-ji'''|金龍山浅草寺}}, also known as {{Nihongo|'''Asakusa Kannon'''|浅草観音}}}}, is an ancient {{ill|Buddhist temples in Japan|en|Buddhist temples in Japan|WD=Q3141900|lt=Buddhist temple}} in [[Asakusa]], Tokyo, Japan. It is Tokyo's oldest-established temple, and one of its most significant. It is dedicated to [[Kannon|Kannon]], the {{ill|Bodhisattva|en|Bodhisattva|WD=Q178149|lt=Bodhisattva}} of compassion. Structures in the temple complex include the main hall, a five-story {{ill|Pagoda|en|Pagoda|WD=Q199451|lt=Pagoda}} and large gates. It is the most widely visited religious site in the world with over 30 million visitors annually.{{Cite web |url= http://www.travelandleisure.com/slideshows/worlds-most-visited-sacred-sites |title=World's Most-Visited Sacred Sites}}{{Cite web |url= http://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2014/07/07/national/asakusa-paints-traditional-tokyo-popular-light/#.WNrv7nTyut8 |title = Asakusa paints traditional Tokyo in a popular light|date = 7 July 2014}} The temple was destroyed during a {{ill|Bombing of Tokyo (10 March 1945)|en|Bombing of Tokyo (10 March 1945)|WD=Q51881408|lt=10 March 1945 firebombing air raid on Tokyo}} during {{ill|Pacific War|en|Pacific War|WD=Q184425|lt=Pacific War}}. The main hall was rebuilt in the 1950s. Formerly associated with the {{ill|Tendai|en|Tendai|WD=Q855964|lt=Tendai}} {{ill|Sect|en|Sect|WD=Q19097|lt=Sect}} of {{ill|Buddhism|en|Buddhism|WD=Q748|lt=Buddhism}}, the temple became independent after the war. Leading to it is Nakamise-dōri street, containing many shops with traditional goods.{{Cite web |url= https://planetyze.com/en/japan/tokyo/sensoji-temple |title=Sensoji Temple - Tokyo Travel Guide {{!}} Planetyze|website=Planetyze|language=en|access-date=2017-06-27}} Adjacent to the east of Sensō-ji is the [[Asakusa Shrine]] of the [[Shinto]] religion.{{cite web |url= https://www.gojapango.com/places/tokyo/tokyo/temple/sensoji-temple/ |title=Sensō-ji |publisher=GoJapanGo |access-date=2008-10-23|archive-date=2017-03-28 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20170328043928/https://www.gojapango.com/places/tokyo/tokyo/temple/sensoji-temple/|url-status=dead}} == History == [[File:Dai Nippon Kinryū-zan no Zu, Aōdō Denzen, 1809.jpg|thumb|left|300px|Colored print of Sensō-ji temple, by Aōdō Denzen (亜欧堂田善), circa 1809]] The temple is dedicated to the {{ill|Bodhisattva|en|Bodhisattva|WD=Q178149|lt=Bodhisattva}} [[Kannon|Kannon]] ({{ill|Avalokiteśvara|en|Avalokiteśvara|WD=Q193849|lt=Avalokiteśvara}}). According to legend, a statue of the Kannon was found in the {{ill|Sumida River|en|Sumida River|WD=Q222149|lt=Sumida River}} in 628 AD by two fishermen, brothers Hinokuma Hamanari and Hinokuma Takenari. The chief of their village, Hajino Nakamoto, recognized the sanctity of the statue and enshrined it by remodeling his own house into a small temple in Asakusa so that the villagers could worship Kannon.{{cite web|url=http://www.cse.sc.edu/~jimdavis/Personal/Photographs/Japan2001-SensojiTemple/Sensoji_temple-Sept01.htm|title=Senso-ji (Pure Land) Buddhist Temple, Asakusa, Tokyo, Japan|last=Davis|first=James P.|date=September 2001|publisher=University of South Carolina|access-date=2008-10-23|archive-date=2012-07-29|archive-url=https://archive.today/20120729094515/http://www.cse.sc.edu/~jimdavis/Personal/Photographs/Japan2001-SensojiTemple/Sensoji_temple-Sept01.htm|url-status=dead}} The first temple was founded in 645 AD, which makes it the oldest-established temple in Tokyo.[http://www.worldgreatestsites.com/sensoji.htm World's greatest sites] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080318103100/http://www.worldgreatestsites.com/sensoji.htm |date=2008-03-18 }} accessed May 2, 2008 In the early years of the [[Tokugawa shogunate]], {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|WD=Q171977|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu}} designated Sensō-ji as {{ill|Tutelary deity|en|Tutelary deity|WD=Q3032312|lt=tutelary temple}} of the [[Tokugawa clan]].McClain, James ''et al.'' (1997). [https://books.google.com/books?id=3N5d4xKg7yQC&dq=Sensoji&pg=PA86 ''Edo and Paris,'' p. 86.] During World War II, the temple was destroyed during the {{ill|Bombing of Tokyo (10 March 1945)|en|Bombing of Tokyo (10 March 1945)|WD=Q51881408|lt=10 March 1945 firebombing air raid on Tokyo}}. The main hall was rebuilt in 1951–58 and has been perceived as a symbol of rebirth and peace by Japanese people. In the courtyard there is a tree that was hit by a bomb in the air raids, and it had regrown in the husk of the old tree and is a similar symbol as the temple itself.{{Citation needed|date=December 2023}} The temple now has a titanium tiled roof that maintains a historic image but is stronger and lighter.{{Cite news |url= https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2009/05/25/national/nippon-steel-pitches-roof-tiles-made-of-titanium/ |title=Nippon Steel pitches roof tiles made of titanium |date=2009-05-25|work=The Japan Times Online|access-date=2019-02-18|language=en-US|issn=0447-5763}} The {{ill|Kaminarimon|en|Kaminarimon|WD=Q2378708|lt=Kaminarimon}} gate was rebuilt in 1960, the {{ill|Hōzōmon|en|Hōzōmon|WD=Q2378896|lt=Hōzōmon}} gate in 1964, and the pagoda in 1973.{{cite web |title=Sensoji Temple – The Heart of Asakusa |url= https://www.asakusastation.com/sensoji-temple-the-heart-of-asakusa/ |website=Asakusa Station |access-date=6 March 2024}} The [[Nishinomiya Inari shrine]] was located within the precincts of Sensō-ji and a [[torii]] identified the entry into the hallowed ground of the shrine. A bronze plaque on the gateway structure listed those who contributed to the construction of the torii, which was erected in 1727 (''{{ill|Kyōhō|en|Kyōhō|WD=Q1145048|lt=Kyōhō}} 12, 11th month'').McClain, [https://books.google.com/books?id=-qOuykzxhKUC&dq=Sensoji&pg=PA403 p. 403.] After the {{ill|Government of Meiji Japan|en|Government of Meiji Japan|WD=Q1322181|lt=Meiji government}} ordered the [[shinbutsu bunri|separation of Shinto and Buddhism]] in 1868, the Inari shrine was moved to the grounds of the [[Asakusa Shrine]], where it was destroyed in the 10 March 1945 firebombing.{{cite web |title=Event: Praying for Success in Business at Asakusa Hatsuka-Ebisu 2023 |first= |last= |date=23 January 2023 |url= https://everywhere.tokyo/en/event-asakusa-hatsuka-ebisu-2023/ |work=Tokyo Shitamachi Guide |publisher= |access-date=13 April 2024}} ==Temple grounds== [[File:Sensoji 2012.JPG|thumb|left|The green-roofed shops of Nakamise-dōri leading to the temple]] Sensō-ji is the focus of Tokyo's largest and most popular [[Japanese festivals|festival]], {{ill|Sanja Matsuri|en|Sanja Matsuri|WD=Q219122|lt=Sanja Matsuri}}. This takes place over 3 to 4 days in late spring, and sees the surrounding streets closed to traffic from dawn until late evening.{{Citation needed|date=December 2023}} Dominating the entrance to the temple is the {{ill|Kaminarimon|en|Kaminarimon|WD=Q2378708|lt=Kaminarimon}} or "Thunder Gate". This imposing Buddhist structure features a massive paper lantern dramatically painted in vivid red-and-black tones to suggest thunderclouds and lightning. Beyond the Kaminarimon is Nakamise-dori with its shops, followed by the {{ill|Hōzōmon|en|Hōzōmon|WD=Q2378896|lt=Hōzōmon}} or "Treasure House Gate", which provides the entrance to the inner complex. Within the precincts stand a stately five-story {{ill|Pagoda|en|Pagoda|WD=Q199451|lt=Pagoda}} and the main hall, devoted to Kannon.{{cite web|url=http://www.worldtravelguide.net/attraction/409/attraction_guide/Far-East-Asia/Senso-ji-Temple-Kinryuzan-Senso-ji.html|title=Senso-ji Temple (Kinryuzan Senso-ji) Guide |publisher=World Travel Guide|access-date=2009-02-07}} Many tourists, both Japanese and from abroad, visit Sensō-ji every year. Catering to the visiting crowds, the surrounding area has many traditional shops and eating places that feature traditional dishes (hand-made noodles, sushi, tempura, etc.). Nakamise-Dori, the street leading from the Thunder Gate to the temple itself, is lined with small shops selling souvenirs ranging from fans, ''[[ukiyo-e]]'' ({{ill|Woodblock printing|en|Woodblock printing|WD=Q1261053|lt=woodblock prints}}), {{ill|Kimono|en|Kimono|WD=Q483444|lt=Kimono}} and other robes, Buddhist scrolls, traditional sweets, to {{ill|Godzilla|en|Godzilla|WD=Q6567|lt=Godzilla}} toys, t-shirts and mobile phone straps. These shops themselves are part of a living tradition of selling to pilgrims who walked to Sensō-ji.{{Citation needed|date=December 2023}} Within the temple itself, and also at many places on its approach, there are ''{{ill|O-mikuji|en|O-mikuji|WD=Q1069592|lt=O-mikuji}}'' stalls. For a suggested donation of 100 yen, visitors may consult the oracle and divine answers to their questions. Querents shake labelled sticks from enclosed metal containers and read the corresponding answers they retrieve from one of 100 possible drawers.{{Citation needed|date=December 2023}} Within the temple is a quiet contemplative garden kept in the distinctive {{ill|Japanese garden|en|Japanese garden|WD=Q15835|lt=Japanese style}}.{{Citation needed|date=December 2023}} === Kaminarimon === [[File:Sensoji at night 8.jpg|thumb|right|Kaminarimon. A statue of [[Fūjin]] stands on the right and that of [[Raijin]] on the left.]] The {{nihongo|{{ill|Kaminarimon|en|Kaminarimon|WD=Q2378708|lt=Kaminarimon}}|雷門|"Thunder Gate"}} is the outer of two large entrance gates that ultimately lead to the Sensō-ji (the inner being the Hōzōmon) in [[Asakusa]]. The gate, with its lantern and statues, is popular with tourists. It stands {{convert|11.7|m|ft}} tall, {{convert|11.4|m|ft}} wide and covers an area of {{convert|69.3|m2|sqft}}.{{cite web|url=http://www7.ocn.ne.jp/~sehayama/topics4kaminarimon.htm|language=ja|script-title=ja:雷門|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080224224816/http://www7.ocn.ne.jp/~sehayama/topics4kaminarimon.htm|archive-date=February 24, 2008|url-status=dead|access-date=2008-03-07|df=mdy-all}} The first gate was built in 941, but the current gate dates back to 1960, after the previous gate was destroyed in a fire in 1865.{{Citation needed|date=December 2023}} ==== History ==== The Kaminarimon was first built in 941 AD by [[Taira clan|Taira]] no Kinmasa, a military commander.{{cite web|url=http://www.taitocity.com/kanko/asakusa_ueno/e_guide/tour/spots/kaminarimon.html|title=Kaminarimon Gate|access-date=2008-03-07|archive-date=2008-03-18|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080318103831/http://www.taitocity.com/kanko/asakusa_ueno/e_guide/tour/spots/kaminarimon.html|url-status=dead}} It was originally located near Komagata, but it was reconstructed in its current location in 1635. This is believed to be when the gods of wind and thunder were first placed on the gate. The gate has been destroyed many times throughout the ages. Four years after its relocation, the Kaminarimon burned down, and in 1649 AD {{ill|Tokugawa Iemitsu|en|Tokugawa Iemitsu|WD=Q314481|lt=Tokugawa Iemitsu}} rebuilt the gate along with several other of the major structures in the temple complex.{{cite web|url=http://www.asakusa-umai.ne.jp/e_asakusa/matsuri/matsuri-02_e.html|title=Glossary of Terms|access-date=2008-03-07}} The gate burnt to the ground in 1757 AD and again in 1865 AD. The Kaminarimon's current structure was dedicated in December 1960 AD . Ninety-five years after the last fire, [[:en:Konosuke Matsushita|Konosuke Matsushita]], the founder of Matsushita Electric Industrial Company (now {{ill|Panasonic|en|Panasonic|WD=Q53247|lt=Panasonic}}), was asked to rebuild the gate. With monetary donations from Matsushita, it was rebuilt in 1960.{{cite web|url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2013/11/18/national/famed-kaminarimon-lantern-gets-rare-makeover/|title=Famed Kaminarimon lantern gets rare makeover|date=November 18, 2013|work=[[The Japan Times]]|access-date=March 22, 2019|agency=[[Kyodo News]]}} ==== Features ==== [[File:Kaminarimon_lantern_bottom_2006.JPG|right|thumb|The wooden carving of a {{ill|Japanese dragon|en|Japanese dragon|WD=Q2366503|lt=dragon}} on the bottom of the great red {{ill|paper lantern|en|paper lantern|WD=Q9545439|lt=lantern}} on the Kaminarimon]] Four statues are housed in the Kaminarimon, two in the front alcoves and two on the other side. On the front of the gate, the statues of the [[Shinto]] gods [[Fūjin]] and [[Raijin]] are displayed. Fūjin, the god of wind, is located on the east side of the gate, while Raijin, the god of thunder, is located on the west side. The original sculptures were severely damaged in the fire of 1865, with only the heads being saved, and the statues restored for the gate's 1960 reconstruction.Enbutsu, Sumiko. ''Old Tokyo: Walks in the City of the Shogun''. Tokyo: Tuttle, 2012 Two additional statues stand on the reverse of the gate: the {{ill|Buddhism|en|Buddhism|WD=Q748|lt=Buddhist}} god Tenryū on the east, and the goddess Kinryū on the west side. These were donated in 1978 to commemorate the 1350th anniversary of the first appearance of the {{ill|Bodhisattva|en|Bodhisattva|WD=Q178149|lt=Bodhisattva}} [[Kannon|Kannon]] ({{ill|Avalokiteśvara|en|Avalokiteśvara|WD=Q193849|lt=Avalokiteśvara}}) at Asakusa, which led to the founding of Sensō-ji. The statues were carved by then-106-year-old master sculptor {{ill|Hirakushi Denchū|en|Hirakushi Denchū|WD=Q11483145|lt=Hirakushi Denchū}}. A giant red lantern (''[[Traditional lighting equipment of Japan#Chōchin|chōchin]]'') hangs under the center of the gate. It is {{convert|3.9|m|ft}} tall, {{convert|3.3|m|ft}} wide and weighs approximately {{convert|700|kg|lb}}. The current lantern, the fifth iteration, was built by Takahashi Chōchin K.K in 2013 and has the same metallic base on the bottom as the previous lantern. The base has a name plate that says "Matsushita Denki", an abbreviated form of Panasonic's old Japanese name, Matsushita Denki Sangyo Kabushiki Gaisha. The front of the lantern displays the gate's name, {{nihongo|Kaminarimon|雷門}}. Painted on the back is the gate's official name, {{nihongo|Fūraijinmon|風雷神門}}.{{cite web|url=http://www.asakusa-e.com/rekisi/senso_e.htm|title=Sensoji Temple|access-date=2008-03-07}} During festivals such as {{ill|Sanja Matsuri|en|Sanja Matsuri|WD=Q219122|lt=Sanja Matsuri}}, the lantern is collapsed to let tall objects pass through the gate. The characters {{Nihongo|金龍山|Kinryū-zan}} on the tablet above the lantern read from right to left and reference the Sensō-ji. === Hōzōmon === [[File:Hozomon_on_an_overcast_day_dllu.jpg|right|thumb|The south face of the Hōzōmon]] The {{nihongo|{{ill|Hōzōmon|en|Hōzōmon|WD=Q2378896|lt=Hōzōmon}}|宝蔵門|"Treasure-House Gate"}} is the inner of two large entrance gates that lead to the Sensō-ji. It is a two-story gate (''{{ill|Nijūmon|en|Nijūmon|WD=Q3341490|lt=Nijūmon}}''), and its second story houses many of the Sensō-ji's treasures. The first story houses two statues, three lanterns and two large sandals. It stands {{convert|22.7|m|ft}} tall, {{convert|21|m|ft}} wide, and {{convert|8|m|ft}} deep.{{cite web|url=http://www7.ocn.ne.jp/~sehayama/topics6houzou5juu.htm|language=ja|script-title=ja:宝蔵門・五重搭・不動尊|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080229002310/http://www7.ocn.ne.jp/~sehayama/topics6houzou5juu.htm|archive-date=2008-02-29|url-status=dead|access-date=2008-03-30}} ==== History ==== [[File:Hozomon_sensoji_back.jpg|thumb|The gate's north face]] The Hōzōmon was first built in 942 AD by [[Taira clan|Taira]] no Kinmasa.{{cite web|url=http://www.asakusa-e.com/rekisi/senso_e.htm|title=Sensoji Temple|work=asakusa-e.com|access-date=2008-03-30}} Destroyed by fire in 1631, it was rebuilt by {{ill|Tokugawa Iemitsu|en|Tokugawa Iemitsu|WD=Q314481|lt=Tokugawa Iemitsu}} in 1636. It stood for 300 more years until it was once again burned down during the [[:en:Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of 1945]]. In 1964, the present steel-reinforced concrete structure was built with a donation of [[:en:Yen|¥]]150 million from Yonetarō Motoya. Since the gate was reconstructed using flame-resistant materials, the upper story of the Hōzōmon stores the Sensō-ji's treasured {{ill|Sutra|en|Sutra|WD=Q209680|lt=sutras}}. These treasures include a copy of the {{ill|en:Lotus Sutra|en|en:Lotus Sutra|WD=Q861212|lt=en:Lotus Sutra}} that is designated a [[:en:National treasures of Japan|Japanese National Treasure]] and the ''Issai-kyō'', a complete collection of {{ill|Buddhism|en|Buddhism|WD=Q748|lt=Buddhist}} scriptures that has been designated an {{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|en|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|WD=Q1188622|lt=Important Cultural Property}}.{{cite web|url=http://www.asakusa-umai.ne.jp/e_asakusa/matsuri/matsuri-02_e.html|title=Glossary of Terms|access-date=2008-03-30}} ==== Features ==== [[File:Shukongoshin.JPG|thumb|One of the {{ill|Nio (Buddhism)|en|Nio (Buddhism)|WD=Q539715|lt=Nio (Buddhism)}} statues that stand on either side of the gate's south face]] Unlike the Kaminarimon, which houses four different statues, the Hōzōmon houses two guardian statues that are located on either side of the gate's south face. These {{convert|5.45|m|ft}} tall statues represent {{ill|Nio (Buddhism)|en|Nio (Buddhism)|WD=Q539715|lt=Nio (Buddhism)}}, the guardian deities of the [[:en:Gautama Buddha|Buddha]]. Because of these statues, the gate was originally called the {{nihongo|''{{ill|Niōmon|en|Niōmon|WD=Q3342330|lt=Niōmon}}''|仁王門|"Niō Gate"}} before it was renamed the Hōzōmon. The gate also features three large lanterns. The largest and most prominent lantern is a red ''[[Traditional lighting equipment of Japan#Chōchin|chōchin]]'' that hangs under the center of the gate's opening. With a height of {{convert|3.75|m|ft}}, a diameter of {{convert|2.7|m|ft}} and a weight of {{convert|400|kg|lbs}}, the lantern displays the name of the town {{nihongo|Kobunachō|小舟町}}. The current iteration of the lantern dates back to 2003 when ¥2 billion was donated by the people of Kobunachō. Its donation commemorated the 10th-year-anniversary of the start of the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}. On either side of the ''chōchin'' hangs five {{convert|2.75|m|ft}} tall copper ''[[Traditional lighting equipment of Japan#Tōrō|tōrō]]'' weighing approximately {{convert|1000|kg|lbs}} each. All three lanterns are completely removed during festivals such as {{ill|Sanja Matsuri|en|Sanja Matsuri|WD=Q219122|lt=Sanja Matsuri}}. On the Hōzōmon's east (back) face are the ''{{ill|Waraji|en|Waraji|WD=Q696696|lt=Waraji}}'', two {{convert|4.5|m|ft}} long, {{convert|1.5|m|ft}} wide straw sandals that weigh {{convert|400|kg|lbs}} each.{{cite web|url=http://www7.ocn.ne.jp/~sehayama/oteratojinnja.htm|language=ja|script-title=ja:浅草神社と浅草寺の説明|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080207085132/http://www7.ocn.ne.jp/~sehayama/oteratojinnja.htm|archive-date=2008-02-07|url-status=dead|access-date=2008-03-30}} ==Nakamise-dōri== [[File:Nakamise dori.jpg|thumb|Nakamise-dōri at night]] [[File:Nakamise street 2020-04-19.jpg|thumb|Nakamise-dōri under the state of emergency for coronavirus pandemic in 2020]] The {{nihongo|'''Nakamise-dōri'''|仲見世通り||}} is a street on the approach to the temple. It is said to have come about in the early 12th century, when neighbors of Sensō-ji were granted permission to set up shops on the approach to the temple. However, in May 1885 the government of Tokyo ordered all shop owners to leave. In December of that same year the area was reconstructed in Western-style brick. During the [[:en:1923 Great Kantō earthquake|1923 Great Kantō earthquake]] many of the shops were destroyed, then rebuilt in 1925 using concrete, only to be destroyed again during the bombings of World War II. The street is approximately {{convert|250|m|ft}} long and contains around 72 shops.[http://www.asakusa-nakamise.jp/e-index.html Asakusa-Nakamise:] [http://www.asakusa-nakamise.jp/e-history.html History of Nakamise.] ==Gallery== File:Nakamise1411.jpg|Pilgrims and tourists flocking to Sensō-ji have shopped at the small stores here for centuries. File:Sensoji at night.JPG|The temple during nighttime File:Asakusa - Senso-ji 35 (15576702197).jpg File:Sensō-ji - Ceiling - August 2013 - Sarah Stierch 02.JPG File:Sensoji Dragon Fountain.JPG File:Sensoji temple meiji era monochrome1910.jpg|1910 File:Toto_Kinryuzan_Senso-ji_zu_02.jpg|1820 File:100 views edo 039.jpg|[[Hiroshige]] File:View of mikoshi from sensoji Sanja Matsuri 2006-3.jpg|{{ill|Sanja Matsuri|en|Sanja Matsuri|WD=Q219122|lt=Sanja Matsuri}} File:Bosatsu Kannon from Simida River 02.JPG|An illustration window in Sensoji of how the two fishermen brothers find {{ill|Bosatsu|en|Bosatsu|WD=Q23925162|lt=Bosatsu}} [[Kannon]] statuette in {{ill|Sumida River|en|Sumida River|WD=Q222149|lt=Sumida River}} File:Bosatsu Kannon from Simida River 01.JPG|An illustration window in Sensoji of {{ill|Bosatsu|en|Bosatsu|WD=Q23925162|lt=Bosatsu}} [[Kannon]] consecrated and worshiped in early Senso-ji and [[Asakusa Shrine]] File:Photo-TokyoAirRaids-1945-3-10-Destroyed Nakamise-4.png|Nakamise-Dori after the American bombings of 1945 == See also == * {{ill|Buddhist temples in Japan|en|Buddhist temples in Japan|WD=Q3141900|lt=Buddhist temples in Japan}} * [[Glossary of Japanese Buddhism]] * {{ill|List of Buddhist temples|en|List of Buddhist temples|WD=Q6808012|lt=List of Buddhist temples}} * [[:en:en:List of National Treasures of Japan (writings)|en:List of National Treasures of Japan (writings)]] == Notes == {{Reflist}} ==References== * McClain, James L., John M. Merriman, Kaoru Ugawa and Ugawa Kaoru. (1997). [https://books.google.com/books?id=-qOuykzxhKUC ''Edo and Paris: Urban Life and the State in the Early Modern Era.''] Ithaca: {{ill|Cornell University Press|en|Cornell University Press|WD=Q2997531|lt=Cornell University Press}}. {{ISBN|978-0-8014-8183-3}}; [http://www.worldcat.org/wcpa/oclc/39088759 OCLC 39088759] ==External links== {{Commons Category|Sensoji|Sensō-ji}} * {{Official website|https://www.senso-ji.jp/english/}} {{Buddhist temples in Japan}} {{Taitō, Tokyo}}]]]] [[en:Sensō-ji]] [[arz:سينسو جى]] [[de:Sensō-ji]] [[el:Σένσο-τζι]] [[es:Sensō-ji]] [[eu:Sensō-ji]] [[fa:معبد سنسوجی]] [[fi:Sensō-ji]] [[fr:Sensō-ji]] [[gl:Sensō-ji]] [[hi:सेन्सो-जी]] [[hu:Szenszódzsi]] [[id:Sensō-ji]] [[it:Sensō-ji]] [[ja:浅草寺]] [[ko:센소지]] [[pl:Sensō-ji]] [[pt:Templo Sensoji]] [[ro:Sensō-ji]] [[ru:Сэнсо-дзи]] [[sh:Sensō-ji]] [[simple:Sensō-ji]] [[sl:Senso-dži]] [[sv:Sensoji]] [[th:เซ็นโซจิ]] [[tr:Sensō-ji]] [[uk:Монастир Сенсо]] [[vi:Chùa Sensō]] [[war:Sensō-ji]] [[zh:淺草寺]] [[zh-min-nan:Chhián-chháu-sī]] {{wikidata link|Q615183}} [[Category:Asakusa]] [[Category:Buddhist temples in Tokyo]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Japan destroyed during World War II]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Taitō]] [[Category:Pages with simple english wikipedia interwikis]] [[Category:Temples of Avalokiteśvara]] [[Category:Tokyo Metropolitan Designated Tangible Cultural Property]] [[Category:qq]] [[Category:Wikidata has short description]] [[Category:Pages with unclosed square brackets]]

{{ill|Hinokuma no Hamanari|WD=Q123219585}}; {{ill|Hinokuma no Takenari|WD=Q123219599}}|deity={{ill|Avalokiteśvara|WD=Q193849}}|part_of={{ill|Bandō Sanjūsankasho|WD=Q806417}}; {{ill|Edo Sanjūsankasho|WD=Q11550981}}; {{ill|Q11557223|WD=Q11557223}}; {{ill|Three Major Kannon Temples in Japan|WD=Q11507116}}}}{{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q615183]] Wikidata name: Sensō-ji [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:12, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Short description|Buddhist temple in Tokyo, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Sensō-ji | native_name = | image = Sensoji 2023.jpg | alt = | caption = Sensō-ji Main Hall in 2023 | map_type = Japan | map_size = | map_alt = | map_caption = | location = 2-3-1 Asakusa, [[:en:Taitō, Tokyo|Taitō-ku, Tokyo]] | coordinates = {{coord|35.714722|139.79675|type:landmark|display=title,inline}} | religious_affiliation = {{ill|Buddhism|en|Buddhism|WD=Q748|lt=Buddhism}} | sect = Shō-Kannon (independent school) | deity = {{ill|Avalokiteśvara|en|Avalokiteśvara|WD=Q193849|lt=Shō Kannon Bosatsu}}
(Āryāvalokiteśvara) | country = Japan | functional_status = | website = {{URL|www.senso-ji.jp}} | founded_by = Kaishō | year_completed = 645 }} {{nihongo|'''Sensō-ji'''|浅草寺 {{IPA|ja|sẽ̞ꜜɰ̃so̞ːʑi||TomJ-SensoJi.ogg}}|Sensō-ji|4=officially {{Nihongo|'''Kinryū-zan Sensō-ji'''|金龍山浅草寺}}, also known as {{Nihongo|'''Asakusa Kannon'''|浅草観音}}}}, is an ancient {{ill|Buddhist temples in Japan|en|Buddhist temples in Japan|WD=Q3141900|lt=Buddhist temple}} in [[Asakusa]], Tokyo, Japan. It is Tokyo's oldest-established temple, and one of its most significant. It is dedicated to [[Kannon|Kannon]], the {{ill|Bodhisattva|en|Bodhisattva|WD=Q178149|lt=Bodhisattva}} of compassion. Structures in the temple complex include the main hall, a five-story {{ill|Pagoda|en|Pagoda|WD=Q199451|lt=Pagoda}} and large gates. It is the most widely visited religious site in the world with over 30 million visitors annually.{{Cite web |url= http://www.travelandleisure.com/slideshows/worlds-most-visited-sacred-sites |title=World's Most-Visited Sacred Sites}}{{Cite web |url= http://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2014/07/07/national/asakusa-paints-traditional-tokyo-popular-light/#.WNrv7nTyut8 |title = Asakusa paints traditional Tokyo in a popular light|date = 7 July 2014}} The temple was destroyed during a {{ill|Bombing of Tokyo (10 March 1945)|en|Bombing of Tokyo (10 March 1945)|WD=Q51881408|lt=10 March 1945 firebombing air raid on Tokyo}} during {{ill|Pacific War|en|Pacific War|WD=Q184425|lt=Pacific War}}. The main hall was rebuilt in the 1950s. Formerly associated with the {{ill|Tendai|en|Tendai|WD=Q855964|lt=Tendai}} {{ill|Sect|en|Sect|WD=Q19097|lt=Sect}} of {{ill|Buddhism|en|Buddhism|WD=Q748|lt=Buddhism}}, the temple became independent after the war. Leading to it is Nakamise-dōri street, containing many shops with traditional goods.{{Cite web |url= https://planetyze.com/en/japan/tokyo/sensoji-temple |title=Sensoji Temple - Tokyo Travel Guide {{!}} Planetyze|website=Planetyze|language=en|access-date=2017-06-27}} Adjacent to the east of Sensō-ji is the [[Asakusa Shrine]] of the [[Shinto]] religion.{{cite web |url= https://www.gojapango.com/places/tokyo/tokyo/temple/sensoji-temple/ |title=Sensō-ji |publisher=GoJapanGo |access-date=2008-10-23|archive-date=2017-03-28 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20170328043928/https://www.gojapango.com/places/tokyo/tokyo/temple/sensoji-temple/|url-status=dead}} == History == [[File:Dai Nippon Kinryū-zan no Zu, Aōdō Denzen, 1809.jpg|thumb|left|300px|Colored print of Sensō-ji temple, by Aōdō Denzen (亜欧堂田善), circa 1809]] The temple is dedicated to the {{ill|Bodhisattva|en|Bodhisattva|WD=Q178149|lt=Bodhisattva}} [[Kannon|Kannon]] ({{ill|Avalokiteśvara|en|Avalokiteśvara|WD=Q193849|lt=Avalokiteśvara}}). According to legend, a statue of the Kannon was found in the {{ill|Sumida River|en|Sumida River|WD=Q222149|lt=Sumida River}} in 628 AD by two fishermen, brothers Hinokuma Hamanari and Hinokuma Takenari. The chief of their village, Hajino Nakamoto, recognized the sanctity of the statue and enshrined it by remodeling his own house into a small temple in Asakusa so that the villagers could worship Kannon.{{cite web|url=http://www.cse.sc.edu/~jimdavis/Personal/Photographs/Japan2001-SensojiTemple/Sensoji_temple-Sept01.htm|title=Senso-ji (Pure Land) Buddhist Temple, Asakusa, Tokyo, Japan|last=Davis|first=James P.|date=September 2001|publisher=University of South Carolina|access-date=2008-10-23|archive-date=2012-07-29|archive-url=https://archive.today/20120729094515/http://www.cse.sc.edu/~jimdavis/Personal/Photographs/Japan2001-SensojiTemple/Sensoji_temple-Sept01.htm|url-status=dead}} The first temple was founded in 645 AD, which makes it the oldest-established temple in Tokyo.[http://www.worldgreatestsites.com/sensoji.htm World's greatest sites] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080318103100/http://www.worldgreatestsites.com/sensoji.htm |date=2008-03-18 }} accessed May 2, 2008 In the early years of the [[Tokugawa shogunate]], {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|WD=Q171977|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu}} designated Sensō-ji as {{ill|Tutelary deity|en|Tutelary deity|WD=Q3032312|lt=tutelary temple}} of the [[Tokugawa clan]].McClain, James ''et al.'' (1997). [https://books.google.com/books?id=3N5d4xKg7yQC&dq=Sensoji&pg=PA86 ''Edo and Paris,'' p. 86.] During World War II, the temple was destroyed during the {{ill|Bombing of Tokyo (10 March 1945)|en|Bombing of Tokyo (10 March 1945)|WD=Q51881408|lt=10 March 1945 firebombing air raid on Tokyo}}. The main hall was rebuilt in 1951–58 and has been perceived as a symbol of rebirth and peace by Japanese people. In the courtyard there is a tree that was hit by a bomb in the air raids, and it had regrown in the husk of the old tree and is a similar symbol as the temple itself.{{Citation needed|date=December 2023}} The temple now has a titanium tiled roof that maintains a historic image but is stronger and lighter.{{Cite news |url= https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2009/05/25/national/nippon-steel-pitches-roof-tiles-made-of-titanium/ |title=Nippon Steel pitches roof tiles made of titanium |date=2009-05-25|work=The Japan Times Online|access-date=2019-02-18|language=en-US|issn=0447-5763}} The {{ill|Kaminarimon|en|Kaminarimon|WD=Q2378708|lt=Kaminarimon}} gate was rebuilt in 1960, the {{ill|Hōzōmon|en|Hōzōmon|WD=Q2378896|lt=Hōzōmon}} gate in 1964, and the pagoda in 1973.{{cite web |title=Sensoji Temple – The Heart of Asakusa |url= https://www.asakusastation.com/sensoji-temple-the-heart-of-asakusa/ |website=Asakusa Station |access-date=6 March 2024}} The [[Nishinomiya Inari shrine]] was located within the precincts of Sensō-ji and a [[torii]] identified the entry into the hallowed ground of the shrine. A bronze plaque on the gateway structure listed those who contributed to the construction of the torii, which was erected in 1727 (''{{ill|Kyōhō|en|Kyōhō|WD=Q1145048|lt=Kyōhō}} 12, 11th month'').McClain, [https://books.google.com/books?id=-qOuykzxhKUC&dq=Sensoji&pg=PA403 p. 403.] After the {{ill|Government of Meiji Japan|en|Government of Meiji Japan|WD=Q1322181|lt=Meiji government}} ordered the [[shinbutsu bunri|separation of Shinto and Buddhism]] in 1868, the Inari shrine was moved to the grounds of the [[Asakusa Shrine]], where it was destroyed in the 10 March 1945 firebombing.{{cite web |title=Event: Praying for Success in Business at Asakusa Hatsuka-Ebisu 2023 |first= |last= |date=23 January 2023 |url= https://everywhere.tokyo/en/event-asakusa-hatsuka-ebisu-2023/ |work=Tokyo Shitamachi Guide |publisher= |access-date=13 April 2024}} ==Temple grounds== [[File:Sensoji 2012.JPG|thumb|left|The green-roofed shops of Nakamise-dōri leading to the temple]] Sensō-ji is the focus of Tokyo's largest and most popular [[Japanese festivals|festival]], {{ill|Sanja Matsuri|en|Sanja Matsuri|WD=Q219122|lt=Sanja Matsuri}}. This takes place over 3 to 4 days in late spring, and sees the surrounding streets closed to traffic from dawn until late evening.{{Citation needed|date=December 2023}} Dominating the entrance to the temple is the {{ill|Kaminarimon|en|Kaminarimon|WD=Q2378708|lt=Kaminarimon}} or "Thunder Gate". This imposing Buddhist structure features a massive paper lantern dramatically painted in vivid red-and-black tones to suggest thunderclouds and lightning. Beyond the Kaminarimon is Nakamise-dori with its shops, followed by the {{ill|Hōzōmon|en|Hōzōmon|WD=Q2378896|lt=Hōzōmon}} or "Treasure House Gate", which provides the entrance to the inner complex. Within the precincts stand a stately five-story {{ill|Pagoda|en|Pagoda|WD=Q199451|lt=Pagoda}} and the main hall, devoted to Kannon.{{cite web|url=http://www.worldtravelguide.net/attraction/409/attraction_guide/Far-East-Asia/Senso-ji-Temple-Kinryuzan-Senso-ji.html|title=Senso-ji Temple (Kinryuzan Senso-ji) Guide |publisher=World Travel Guide|access-date=2009-02-07}} Many tourists, both Japanese and from abroad, visit Sensō-ji every year. Catering to the visiting crowds, the surrounding area has many traditional shops and eating places that feature traditional dishes (hand-made noodles, sushi, tempura, etc.). Nakamise-Dori, the street leading from the Thunder Gate to the temple itself, is lined with small shops selling souvenirs ranging from fans, ''[[ukiyo-e]]'' ({{ill|Woodblock printing|en|Woodblock printing|WD=Q1261053|lt=woodblock prints}}), {{ill|Kimono|en|Kimono|WD=Q483444|lt=Kimono}} and other robes, Buddhist scrolls, traditional sweets, to {{ill|Godzilla|en|Godzilla|WD=Q6567|lt=Godzilla}} toys, t-shirts and mobile phone straps. These shops themselves are part of a living tradition of selling to pilgrims who walked to Sensō-ji.{{Citation needed|date=December 2023}} Within the temple itself, and also at many places on its approach, there are ''{{ill|O-mikuji|en|O-mikuji|WD=Q1069592|lt=O-mikuji}}'' stalls. For a suggested donation of 100 yen, visitors may consult the oracle and divine answers to their questions. Querents shake labelled sticks from enclosed metal containers and read the corresponding answers they retrieve from one of 100 possible drawers.{{Citation needed|date=December 2023}} Within the temple is a quiet contemplative garden kept in the distinctive {{ill|Japanese garden|en|Japanese garden|WD=Q15835|lt=Japanese style}}.{{Citation needed|date=December 2023}} === Kaminarimon === [[File:Sensoji at night 8.jpg|thumb|right|Kaminarimon. A statue of [[Fūjin]] stands on the right and that of [[Raijin]] on the left.]] The {{nihongo|{{ill|Kaminarimon|en|Kaminarimon|WD=Q2378708|lt=Kaminarimon}}|雷門|"Thunder Gate"}} is the outer of two large entrance gates that ultimately lead to the Sensō-ji (the inner being the Hōzōmon) in [[Asakusa]]. The gate, with its lantern and statues, is popular with tourists. It stands {{convert|11.7|m|ft}} tall, {{convert|11.4|m|ft}} wide and covers an area of {{convert|69.3|m2|sqft}}.{{cite web|url=http://www7.ocn.ne.jp/~sehayama/topics4kaminarimon.htm|language=ja|script-title=ja:雷門|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080224224816/http://www7.ocn.ne.jp/~sehayama/topics4kaminarimon.htm|archive-date=February 24, 2008|url-status=dead|access-date=2008-03-07|df=mdy-all}} The first gate was built in 941, but the current gate dates back to 1960, after the previous gate was destroyed in a fire in 1865.{{Citation needed|date=December 2023}} ==== History ==== The Kaminarimon was first built in 941 AD by [[Taira clan|Taira]] no Kinmasa, a military commander.{{cite web|url=http://www.taitocity.com/kanko/asakusa_ueno/e_guide/tour/spots/kaminarimon.html|title=Kaminarimon Gate|access-date=2008-03-07|archive-date=2008-03-18|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080318103831/http://www.taitocity.com/kanko/asakusa_ueno/e_guide/tour/spots/kaminarimon.html|url-status=dead}} It was originally located near Komagata, but it was reconstructed in its current location in 1635. This is believed to be when the gods of wind and thunder were first placed on the gate. The gate has been destroyed many times throughout the ages. Four years after its relocation, the Kaminarimon burned down, and in 1649 AD {{ill|Tokugawa Iemitsu|en|Tokugawa Iemitsu|WD=Q314481|lt=Tokugawa Iemitsu}} rebuilt the gate along with several other of the major structures in the temple complex.{{cite web|url=http://www.asakusa-umai.ne.jp/e_asakusa/matsuri/matsuri-02_e.html|title=Glossary of Terms|access-date=2008-03-07}} The gate burnt to the ground in 1757 AD and again in 1865 AD. The Kaminarimon's current structure was dedicated in December 1960 AD . Ninety-five years after the last fire, [[:en:Konosuke Matsushita|Konosuke Matsushita]], the founder of Matsushita Electric Industrial Company (now {{ill|Panasonic|en|Panasonic|WD=Q53247|lt=Panasonic}}), was asked to rebuild the gate. With monetary donations from Matsushita, it was rebuilt in 1960.{{cite web|url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2013/11/18/national/famed-kaminarimon-lantern-gets-rare-makeover/|title=Famed Kaminarimon lantern gets rare makeover|date=November 18, 2013|work=[[The Japan Times]]|access-date=March 22, 2019|agency=[[Kyodo News]]}} ==== Features ==== [[File:Kaminarimon_lantern_bottom_2006.JPG|right|thumb|The wooden carving of a {{ill|Japanese dragon|en|Japanese dragon|WD=Q2366503|lt=dragon}} on the bottom of the great red {{ill|paper lantern|en|paper lantern|WD=Q9545439|lt=lantern}} on the Kaminarimon]] Four statues are housed in the Kaminarimon, two in the front alcoves and two on the other side. On the front of the gate, the statues of the [[Shinto]] gods [[Fūjin]] and [[Raijin]] are displayed. Fūjin, the god of wind, is located on the east side of the gate, while Raijin, the god of thunder, is located on the west side. The original sculptures were severely damaged in the fire of 1865, with only the heads being saved, and the statues restored for the gate's 1960 reconstruction.Enbutsu, Sumiko. ''Old Tokyo: Walks in the City of the Shogun''. Tokyo: Tuttle, 2012 Two additional statues stand on the reverse of the gate: the {{ill|Buddhism|en|Buddhism|WD=Q748|lt=Buddhist}} god Tenryū on the east, and the goddess Kinryū on the west side. These were donated in 1978 to commemorate the 1350th anniversary of the first appearance of the {{ill|Bodhisattva|en|Bodhisattva|WD=Q178149|lt=Bodhisattva}} [[Kannon|Kannon]] ({{ill|Avalokiteśvara|en|Avalokiteśvara|WD=Q193849|lt=Avalokiteśvara}}) at Asakusa, which led to the founding of Sensō-ji. The statues were carved by then-106-year-old master sculptor {{ill|Hirakushi Denchū|en|Hirakushi Denchū|WD=Q11483145|lt=Hirakushi Denchū}}. A giant red lantern (''[[Traditional lighting equipment of Japan#Chōchin|chōchin]]'') hangs under the center of the gate. It is {{convert|3.9|m|ft}} tall, {{convert|3.3|m|ft}} wide and weighs approximately {{convert|700|kg|lb}}. The current lantern, the fifth iteration, was built by Takahashi Chōchin K.K in 2013 and has the same metallic base on the bottom as the previous lantern. The base has a name plate that says "Matsushita Denki", an abbreviated form of Panasonic's old Japanese name, Matsushita Denki Sangyo Kabushiki Gaisha. The front of the lantern displays the gate's name, {{nihongo|Kaminarimon|雷門}}. Painted on the back is the gate's official name, {{nihongo|Fūraijinmon|風雷神門}}.{{cite web|url=http://www.asakusa-e.com/rekisi/senso_e.htm|title=Sensoji Temple|access-date=2008-03-07}} During festivals such as {{ill|Sanja Matsuri|en|Sanja Matsuri|WD=Q219122|lt=Sanja Matsuri}}, the lantern is collapsed to let tall objects pass through the gate. The characters {{Nihongo|金龍山|Kinryū-zan}} on the tablet above the lantern read from right to left and reference the Sensō-ji. === Hōzōmon === [[File:Hozomon_on_an_overcast_day_dllu.jpg|right|thumb|The south face of the Hōzōmon]] The {{nihongo|{{ill|Hōzōmon|en|Hōzōmon|WD=Q2378896|lt=Hōzōmon}}|宝蔵門|"Treasure-House Gate"}} is the inner of two large entrance gates that lead to the Sensō-ji. It is a two-story gate (''{{ill|Nijūmon|en|Nijūmon|WD=Q3341490|lt=Nijūmon}}''), and its second story houses many of the Sensō-ji's treasures. The first story houses two statues, three lanterns and two large sandals. It stands {{convert|22.7|m|ft}} tall, {{convert|21|m|ft}} wide, and {{convert|8|m|ft}} deep.{{cite web|url=http://www7.ocn.ne.jp/~sehayama/topics6houzou5juu.htm|language=ja|script-title=ja:宝蔵門・五重搭・不動尊|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080229002310/http://www7.ocn.ne.jp/~sehayama/topics6houzou5juu.htm|archive-date=2008-02-29|url-status=dead|access-date=2008-03-30}} ==== History ==== [[File:Hozomon_sensoji_back.jpg|thumb|The gate's north face]] The Hōzōmon was first built in 942 AD by [[Taira clan|Taira]] no Kinmasa.{{cite web|url=http://www.asakusa-e.com/rekisi/senso_e.htm|title=Sensoji Temple|work=asakusa-e.com|access-date=2008-03-30}} Destroyed by fire in 1631, it was rebuilt by {{ill|Tokugawa Iemitsu|en|Tokugawa Iemitsu|WD=Q314481|lt=Tokugawa Iemitsu}} in 1636. It stood for 300 more years until it was once again burned down during the [[:en:Bombing of Tokyo in World War II|Tokyo air raids of 1945]]. In 1964, the present steel-reinforced concrete structure was built with a donation of [[:en:Yen|¥]]150 million from Yonetarō Motoya. Since the gate was reconstructed using flame-resistant materials, the upper story of the Hōzōmon stores the Sensō-ji's treasured {{ill|Sutra|en|Sutra|WD=Q209680|lt=sutras}}. These treasures include a copy of the {{ill|en:Lotus Sutra|en|en:Lotus Sutra|WD=Q861212|lt=en:Lotus Sutra}} that is designated a [[:en:National treasures of Japan|Japanese National Treasure]] and the ''Issai-kyō'', a complete collection of {{ill|Buddhism|en|Buddhism|WD=Q748|lt=Buddhist}} scriptures that has been designated an {{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|en|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|WD=Q1188622|lt=Important Cultural Property}}.{{cite web|url=http://www.asakusa-umai.ne.jp/e_asakusa/matsuri/matsuri-02_e.html|title=Glossary of Terms|access-date=2008-03-30}} ==== Features ==== [[File:Shukongoshin.JPG|thumb|One of the {{ill|Nio (Buddhism)|en|Nio (Buddhism)|WD=Q539715|lt=Nio (Buddhism)}} statues that stand on either side of the gate's south face]] Unlike the Kaminarimon, which houses four different statues, the Hōzōmon houses two guardian statues that are located on either side of the gate's south face. These {{convert|5.45|m|ft}} tall statues represent {{ill|Nio (Buddhism)|en|Nio (Buddhism)|WD=Q539715|lt=Nio (Buddhism)}}, the guardian deities of the [[:en:Gautama Buddha|Buddha]]. Because of these statues, the gate was originally called the {{nihongo|''{{ill|Niōmon|en|Niōmon|WD=Q3342330|lt=Niōmon}}''|仁王門|"Niō Gate"}} before it was renamed the Hōzōmon. The gate also features three large lanterns. The largest and most prominent lantern is a red ''[[Traditional lighting equipment of Japan#Chōchin|chōchin]]'' that hangs under the center of the gate's opening. With a height of {{convert|3.75|m|ft}}, a diameter of {{convert|2.7|m|ft}} and a weight of {{convert|400|kg|lbs}}, the lantern displays the name of the town {{nihongo|Kobunachō|小舟町}}. The current iteration of the lantern dates back to 2003 when ¥2 billion was donated by the people of Kobunachō. Its donation commemorated the 10th-year-anniversary of the start of the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}. On either side of the ''chōchin'' hangs five {{convert|2.75|m|ft}} tall copper ''[[Traditional lighting equipment of Japan#Tōrō|tōrō]]'' weighing approximately {{convert|1000|kg|lbs}} each. All three lanterns are completely removed during festivals such as {{ill|Sanja Matsuri|en|Sanja Matsuri|WD=Q219122|lt=Sanja Matsuri}}. On the Hōzōmon's east (back) face are the ''{{ill|Waraji|en|Waraji|WD=Q696696|lt=Waraji}}'', two {{convert|4.5|m|ft}} long, {{convert|1.5|m|ft}} wide straw sandals that weigh {{convert|400|kg|lbs}} each.{{cite web|url=http://www7.ocn.ne.jp/~sehayama/oteratojinnja.htm|language=ja|script-title=ja:浅草神社と浅草寺の説明|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080207085132/http://www7.ocn.ne.jp/~sehayama/oteratojinnja.htm|archive-date=2008-02-07|url-status=dead|access-date=2008-03-30}} ==Nakamise-dōri== [[File:Nakamise dori.jpg|thumb|Nakamise-dōri at night]] [[File:Nakamise street 2020-04-19.jpg|thumb|Nakamise-dōri under the state of emergency for coronavirus pandemic in 2020]] The {{nihongo|'''Nakamise-dōri'''|仲見世通り||}} is a street on the approach to the temple. It is said to have come about in the early 12th century, when neighbors of Sensō-ji were granted permission to set up shops on the approach to the temple. However, in May 1885 the government of Tokyo ordered all shop owners to leave. In December of that same year the area was reconstructed in Western-style brick. During the [[:en:1923 Great Kantō earthquake|1923 Great Kantō earthquake]] many of the shops were destroyed, then rebuilt in 1925 using concrete, only to be destroyed again during the bombings of World War II. The street is approximately {{convert|250|m|ft}} long and contains around 72 shops.[http://www.asakusa-nakamise.jp/e-index.html Asakusa-Nakamise:] [http://www.asakusa-nakamise.jp/e-history.html History of Nakamise.] ==Gallery== File:Nakamise1411.jpg|Pilgrims and tourists flocking to Sensō-ji have shopped at the small stores here for centuries. File:Sensoji at night.JPG|The temple during nighttime File:Asakusa - Senso-ji 35 (15576702197).jpg File:Sensō-ji - Ceiling - August 2013 - Sarah Stierch 02.JPG File:Sensoji Dragon Fountain.JPG File:Sensoji temple meiji era monochrome1910.jpg|1910 File:Toto_Kinryuzan_Senso-ji_zu_02.jpg|1820 File:100 views edo 039.jpg|[[Hiroshige]] File:View of mikoshi from sensoji Sanja Matsuri 2006-3.jpg|{{ill|Sanja Matsuri|en|Sanja Matsuri|WD=Q219122|lt=Sanja Matsuri}} File:Bosatsu Kannon from Simida River 02.JPG|An illustration window in Sensoji of how the two fishermen brothers find {{ill|Bosatsu|en|Bosatsu|WD=Q23925162|lt=Bosatsu}} [[Kannon]] statuette in {{ill|Sumida River|en|Sumida River|WD=Q222149|lt=Sumida River}} File:Bosatsu Kannon from Simida River 01.JPG|An illustration window in Sensoji of {{ill|Bosatsu|en|Bosatsu|WD=Q23925162|lt=Bosatsu}} [[Kannon]] consecrated and worshiped in early Senso-ji and [[Asakusa Shrine]] File:Photo-TokyoAirRaids-1945-3-10-Destroyed Nakamise-4.png|Nakamise-Dori after the American bombings of 1945 == See also == * {{ill|Buddhist temples in Japan|en|Buddhist temples in Japan|WD=Q3141900|lt=Buddhist temples in Japan}} * [[Glossary of Japanese Buddhism]] * {{ill|List of Buddhist temples|en|List of Buddhist temples|WD=Q6808012|lt=List of Buddhist temples}} * [[:en:en:List of National Treasures of Japan (writings)|en:List of National Treasures of Japan (writings)]] == Notes == {{Reflist}} ==References== * McClain, James L., John M. Merriman, Kaoru Ugawa and Ugawa Kaoru. (1997). [https://books.google.com/books?id=-qOuykzxhKUC ''Edo and Paris: Urban Life and the State in the Early Modern Era.''] Ithaca: {{ill|Cornell University Press|en|Cornell University Press|WD=Q2997531|lt=Cornell University Press}}. {{ISBN|978-0-8014-8183-3}}; [http://www.worldcat.org/wcpa/oclc/39088759 OCLC 39088759] ==External links== {{Commons Category|Sensoji|Sensō-ji}} * {{Official website|https://www.senso-ji.jp/english/}} {{Buddhist temples in Japan}} {{Taitō, Tokyo}}]]]] [[en:Sensō-ji]] [[arz:سينسو جى]] [[de:Sensō-ji]] [[el:Σένσο-τζι]] [[es:Sensō-ji]] [[eu:Sensō-ji]] [[fa:معبد سنسوجی]] [[fi:Sensō-ji]] [[fr:Sensō-ji]] [[gl:Sensō-ji]] [[hi:सेन्सो-जी]] [[hu:Szenszódzsi]] [[id:Sensō-ji]] [[it:Sensō-ji]] [[ja:浅草寺]] [[ko:센소지]] [[pl:Sensō-ji]] [[pt:Templo Sensoji]] [[ro:Sensō-ji]] [[ru:Сэнсо-дзи]] [[sh:Sensō-ji]] [[simple:Sensō-ji]] [[sl:Senso-dži]] [[sv:Sensoji]] [[th:เซ็นโซจิ]] [[tr:Sensō-ji]] [[uk:Монастир Сенсо]] [[vi:Chùa Sensō]] [[war:Sensō-ji]] [[zh:淺草寺]] [[zh-min-nan:Chhián-chháu-sī]] {{wikidata link|Q615183}} [[Category:Asakusa]] [[Category:Buddhist temples in Tokyo]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Japan destroyed during World War II]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Taitō]] [[Category:Pages with simple english wikipedia interwikis]] [[Category:Temples of Avalokiteśvara]] [[Category:Tokyo Metropolitan Designated Tangible Cultural Property]] [[Category:qq]] [[Category:Wikidata has short description]] [[Category:Pages with unclosed square brackets]] [[Category:Pages without translation templates]]
